source: Weisenthal (2023) ChatGPT and post-test probability
finding: ChatGPT wrote Bayes rule correctly when the variables were abstract A, B, C. It made covariate errors once the variables were named Covid, test, cough.
numbers: Task: posterior given a positive test AND a symptom. 20 repeated chats per prompt. Abstract names: formula right 19/20 (95%). Medical names: sensitivity not conditioned on cough 10/20 (50%), pretest not conditioned on cough 12/20 (60%).
limits: One model, one problem type, 20 samples, no human control. The common error is a silent independence assumption (sensitivity treated as fixed across covariates).
agent_relevance: Dressing a probability problem in clinical words lowers accuracy. G5 should move the arithmetic into code and keep the model to extracting numbers.

source: Weisenthal (2023) ChatGPT and post-test probability
finding: Using the terms 'post-test probability', 'sensitivity' and 'specificity' made ChatGPT worse than plain medical names.
numbers: Errors in 20 chats: sensitivity not conditioned on cough 16/20 (80%); pretest not conditioned 17/20 (85%); post-test not conditioned 3/20 (15%); misc probability error 4/20 (20%).
limits: Same single-model, 20-sample design. Authors suspect the diagnostic vocabulary moves the model away from where probability textbooks live.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model do likelihood-ratio arithmetic in diagnostic language. Use a neutral variable schema, then code.

source: Weisenthal (2023) ChatGPT and post-test probability
finding: A stepwise engineered prompt (name disease, test, covariate; write Bayes rule; substitute) removed the conditioning errors.
numbers: With the engineered prompt, Errors 1-3 appeared in 0/20 chats. Correct form with expanded denominator 10/20 (50%) and unexpanded 9/20 (45%); 1/20 still had a denominator error.
limits: Still one model and 20 samples. Residual probability slips remain, and the model sometimes ignores the requested renaming.
agent_relevance: Supports a fixed S7 template that separates term mapping from the algebra. The remaining slip rate argues for code, not prompts, as the final calculator.

source: Rodman et al. (2023) Artificial Intelligence vs Clinician Performance in Estimating Probabilities of Diagnoses Before and After Testing (JAMA Netw Open)
finding: GPT-4 gave pretest and post-negative-test probabilities with less error than 553 clinicians in all 5 primary-care cases. It was better after a positive test in 2 cases, equal in 2, worse in 1.
numbers: LLM n=100 runs vs clinicians n=553 (290 residents, 202 attendings, 61 APPs). Pneumonia pretest: reference 25-42%, LLM median 72, clinicians 80. Breast cancer after positive mammogram: reference 3-9%, LLM 8, clinicians 50 (MAE 4.4 vs 47.5).
limits: Research letter. Five simple vignettes. GPT-4 had a narrower spread than humans; the authors say this likely explains part of the lower error. The median LLM estimate was sometimes farther from the reference than the human median.
agent_relevance: Models start from better priors than clinicians but still miss big on some test-positive cases. A code step using sensitivity and specificity from a table would fix both.

source: Rodman et al. (2023) Artificial Intelligence vs Clinician Performance in Estimating Probabilities of Diagnoses Before and After Testing (JAMA Netw Open)
finding: Both GPT-4 and clinicians massively over-estimated post-positive-test risk for the stress test, a base-rate neglect pattern.
numbers: Cardiac ischemia, after positive stress test, reference 2-11%: LLM median 69% (MAE 56.5), clinicians 70% (MAE 56.2).
limits: One case only. Reference ranges come from a literature review, not a measured population.
agent_relevance: LLMs inherit the human 'positive test means disease' error. Needs an explicit pretest, LR and odds step.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: o1-preview did not clearly beat GPT-4 on pretest and post-test probability estimation. Its gains were elsewhere (differential diagnosis, management).
numbers: Same 5 cases, 100 outputs each for o1-preview and GPT-4, vs 553 clinicians. Pneumonia pretest MAE 31.6 (o1) vs 39.5 (GPT-4) vs 47.7 (clinicians). Cardiac ischemia after positive test: o1 median 10.9 (MAE 5.7) vs GPT-4 68.7 (MAE 56.5), reference 2-11.
limits: The paper says o1 performs similarly to GPT-4 here except the stress test. Pneumonia after negative test: o1 28.5 vs reference 10-19, no better than GPT-4's 25. A reasoning model is not a calibration fix by itself.
agent_relevance: Test-time reasoning helped on one base-rate trap but not generally. Do not rely on 'think longer' for S7 probabilities.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: o1-preview was far better than 2 attendings on real emergency cases and on management, where diagnostic test choice is part of the task.
numbers: Management cases: o1-preview median 86% vs 41% for physicians with GPT-4. ER: 79 cases at 3 touchpoints; gap largest at triage, not significant at admission.
limits: Authors flag benchmark saturation and a weak link to real care. Probabilistic reasoning was one of five experiments and showed no clear gain.
agent_relevance: Test selection gains are real on text benchmarks; calibrated probabilities are the weaker part.

source: Gao et al. (2024) Next-Word Probability Is Not Pre-test Probability
finding: Asked directly for a pretest probability from a patient record, two open LLMs were at chance. A trained classifier on LLM embeddings did far better.
numbers: 660 patients; sepsis, arrhythmia, CHF. Token-logit method mean AUROC 49.9 (95% CI 47.8-51.9); verbalized confidence 50.9 (48.7-53.1). Logit outputs sat only in 0.323-0.337. Embedding + XGB near raw-data XGB for sepsis (AUROC about 71).
limits: Mistral-7B and Llama3-70B only, zero-shot, workshop paper. Frontier models were not tested. Verbalized confidence had the worst calibration (ECE) on CHF.
agent_relevance: The agent must not trust a model's verbal risk number as a prior. Take priors from a table or data, and let the model supply likelihood judgments only.

source: Gao et al. (2024) Next-Word Probability Is Not Pre-test Probability
finding: Adding demographics changed LLM risk estimates in unstable directions.
numbers: Mistral embedding on sepsis: AUROC 71.1 default vs 63.9 with ethnicity added (drop 7.2).
limits: Direction of change varied by task and model; small sample.
agent_relevance: A prior that shifts with irrelevant person details is a guardrail risk. Strip demographics unless the prior needs them.

source: Talboy and Fuller (2023) Challenging the appearance of machine intelligence: Cognitive bias in LLMs and Best Practices for Adoption
finding: On the classic mammography base-rate problem, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 used Bayes rule when numbers were given. With numbers removed, they gave the base rate (10%) instead of the positive predictive value (7.7%).
numbers: Numeric prompt: GPT-3.5 (Mar 2023) and GPT-4 (Aug 2023) correct; GPT-3.5 retest Aug 2023 wrong with no Bayes. Bard Mar 2023 answered the 10% incidence, retest correct. Non-numeric prompt: both GPT models said 10%; Bard said 80% (the sensitivity).
limits: Single-run tests with no sample size. Shows version drift: the same model gave different answers on retest.
agent_relevance: Numbers in the prompt trigger a formula; vague wording triggers the human fallacies. Force explicit numbers into the S7 step.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO)
finding: A scaffold that keeps an explicit probability-ranked differential, picks tests that best separate the leaders, and plays devil's advocate lifted accuracy and cut cost on 304 NEJM cases.
numbers: Physicians (generalists) 19.9% at $2,963 per case. Off-the-shelf o3 78.6% at $7,850. MAI-DxO with o3: 79.9% at $2,397 (budgeted), 81.9% at $4,735 (no budget), ensemble 85.5% at $7,184. GPT-4o baseline 49.3% at $2,745.
limits: Hard NEJM cases only, no healthy patients, so false-positive rates are unknown. The gatekeeper is itself an LLM and invents results for unreported tests. Physicians barred from search and colleagues.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to S7 as a discriminating-test step. Gain is larger for weaker models. Probabilities are model-estimated, not coded, so G5 is not yet used.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO)
finding: The panel has roles for Bayesian-style probability updates after each finding, tests that maximally discriminate, falsification, and cost stewardship. It improved every model tested.
numbers: Significant gains for all tested models (one-sided paired permutation test, 10,000 resamples, p<0.005), except o3 and o4-mini, where the significant result was the cost cut.
limits: I saw no single-role ablation in the text I read. The Bayesian update is done by the LLM in prose, not by code.
agent_relevance: Authors say baseline o3 'seemed to lack a theory of information value'. A coded test-value score is the missing piece.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO)
finding: Off-the-shelf reasoning models order tests that look reasonable for the current differential, not tests that cut uncertainty most per dollar, and they anchor on first impressions.
numbers: Case example: baseline o3 ordered brain MRI and EEG, wrong diagnosis, $3,431; MAI-DxO asked about hand sanitizer ingestion first, right diagnosis, $795.
limits: Authors' inspection of selected cases, not a measured rate.
agent_relevance: Justifies cost-aware discriminating-test selection with a stop rule in S7.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: Choosing each question by expected information gain over simulated answers raised success across 20 Questions, simple diagnosis and troubleshooting.
numbers: Average success-rate gain 38.1% over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs. GPT-4 on DX (5 diseases, closed set): 97.0% vs 91.3% for direct prompting. Llama3-70B DX closed set 83.7 to 90.4. FloDial troubleshooting GPT-4 43.7 to 67.3.
limits: DX test set has only 5 diseases; answers are treated as eliminating sets of possibilities. Authors say 'no fever' is not a hard exclusion and leave Bayesian updating for later. Gains vary: Mistral-Large DX closed set 38.5 to 48.1. Simulates only 3 steps.
agent_relevance: Direct template for the discriminating-test score: expected entropy drop, computed in code on a candidate set.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT beat chain-of-thought, self-consistency, Reflexion and tree-of-thought baselines on the same tasks.
numbers: UoT beat CoT-SC by 33.8% and Reflexion by 29.9% on average success rate; UoT also beat Adapted-ToT by 12.4%.
limits: Gains are on constructed games and simplified dialogues, not real clinical cases.
agent_relevance: Plain reasoning prompts do not give information-seeking skill; an explicit gain objective does.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design (ICLR 2026)
finding: Maximizing expected information gain from the LLM's own predictive distribution improved 20 Questions success by a large margin, and the details of the belief-update step mattered.
numbers: Average gain 37.4 percentage points over direct prompting; success rate more than doubled in over half of the setups and never fell. Movie preference task: smaller gains because Prompt-Only is stronger there.
limits: 20 Questions and preference elicitation only; the answerer is a simulated LLM. The paper says results depend on how the belief update is built. No clinical data.
agent_relevance: Confirms the EIG test choice carries over to new LLMs and that the update step must be designed, not left to the model.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs plateau after one round of evidence and do not update beliefs like a Bayesian. Prompting fixes did not help.
numbers: Flight-choice task, 5 rounds, 624 simulated users. Final-round accuracy of off-the-shelf models roughly 37-58%; Bayesian Assistant 81%. Chain-of-thought, numeric formats, 30 rounds and base models gave no meaningful gain.
limits: Toy preference task. Fine-tuning is a training change, so it is outside our no-training scope.
agent_relevance: Supports putting the evidence update in code (G5): the model cannot be trusted to accumulate evidence over turns.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Fine-tuning on the Bayesian Assistant's own (often wrong) guesses worked better than fine-tuning on the correct answers and generalized to hotel and web-shop tasks.
numbers: Applied to Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B; both fine-tunes beat the originals (p<0.001); Bayesian teaching beat oracle teaching.
limits: Training only; flight and hotel features are simple. The web shop has no exact Bayesian model.
agent_relevance: LLMs hold calibrated uncertainty only if trained on it. For a scaffold-only agent, use a code posterior instead.

source: Li et al. (2024) MediQ: Question-Asking LLMs and a Benchmark for Reliable Interactive Clinical Reasoning
finding: Telling LLMs to ask questions before answering made them worse than answering from the same starting facts.
numbers: Plain interactive prompting dropped accuracy by 11.3% (relative) vs the non-interactive Initial setup. Confidence-gated asking (1-5 scale + rationale + self-consistency x3) raised accuracy 22.3% over plain interactive and 12.1% over Initial. A 10.3% gap to full information remained.
limits: Medical MCQ converted to dialogue with a simulated patient. Self-consistency alone hurt unless combined with rationale. Confidence calibration was poor.
agent_relevance: The stop-or-test decision needs a confidence gate; naive 'ask more' prompts lose accuracy. Matches the test-threshold idea: test only when current belief is below threshold.

source: Li et al. (2025) ALFA: Aligning LLMs to Ask Good Questions, A Case Study in Clinical Reasoning
finding: Training LLMs on fine-grained question attributes (clarity, relevance) improved clinical follow-up questions. Abstract level only.
numbers: Reported: 56.6% fewer diagnostic errors on MediQ-AskDocs vs instruction-tuned baselines; question-level win-rate 64.4%; 17k real interactions, 80k preference pairs.
limits: I read the abstract and first page only. The win-rate judge is an LLM (gpt-4o).
agent_relevance: Supports scoring candidate tests on named attributes, but it is training-based.

source: Tu et al. (2024) Towards Conversational Diagnostic AI (AMIE)
finding: AMIE, a dialogue-tuned LLM, beat primary care physicians on diagnostic accuracy and on 28 of 32 specialist-rated axes in text chat with patient actors. Abstract level only.
numbers: 149 simulated patients; 'superior performance on 28 of 32 axes according to specialist physicians' (abstract).
limits: I skimmed the first pages only. Patient actors, text only. No separate result for likelihood-ratio style test choice.
agent_relevance: Shows history-taking can be built, but gives no direct evidence on test selection.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial (JAMA Netw Open)
finding: Giving doctors access to GPT-4 did not improve their diagnostic reasoning, while GPT-4 alone scored higher than the doctors. Abstract level only.
numbers: 50 physicians, up to 6 vignettes in 60 minutes. Median score 76% (LLM group) vs 74% (conventional), adjusted difference 2 points (95% CI -4 to 8, p=.60). LLM alone scored 16 points above conventional (95% CI 2-30, p=.03).
limits: Abstract read through Europe PMC. Small trial, one month, vignettes.
agent_relevance: The gap is in how people use model output, so a scaffold that runs the test logic itself may matter more than a chat assistant.

source: Berner et al. (1994) Performance of four computer-based diagnostic systems (NEJM)
finding: Older knowledge-based diagnostic programs (DXplain, Iliad, Meditel, QMR) listed the correct diagnosis in about half to seven-tenths of hard cases. Abstract level only.
numbers: 105 hard cases, 10 expert clinicians. Correct-diagnosis proportion 0.52-0.71; relevant diagnoses 0.19-0.37; each program added about 2 extra relevant diagnoses per case that experts had not listed.
limits: Abstract-level read. 1990s systems with manual vocabulary entry. No single program was best on all measures.
agent_relevance: Old systems worked better as idea generators than as deciders. A harvest-all-candidates step (S4) echoes that.

source: Heckerman et al. (1992) An evaluation of the diagnostic accuracy of Pathfinder (Comput Biomed Res)
finding: Pathfinder, a lymph-node pathology system built on probability and decision theory, did better when it modelled dependencies among findings (belief network) than when it assumed all findings independent, and matched the human expert. Abstract level only.
numbers: Two versions compared with informal and decision-theoretic metrics. Dependencies were cost effective; accuracy at least as good as the Pathfinder expert. No sample size in the abstract.
limits: Abstract-level read. Diseases assumed mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
agent_relevance: Parallels the ChatGPT conditional-independence error (Weisenthal): independence is a wrong default for correlated findings.

source: Paruchuri et al. (2024) What Are the Odds? Language Models Are Capable of Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: LLMs can estimate percentiles and probabilities of known distributions, but sample poorly. Examples and real-world context cut errors a lot.
numbers: Zero-shot percentile MAE mean 16.52 (range 0.54 uniform to 28.36); probability MAE mean 21.48. One-shot example gave +59.14% (percentile), +55.26% (sampling K-S), +70.13% (probability) improvement.
limits: Distribution statistics, not medical tests; older models. Gains are relative to zero-shot.
agent_relevance: Anchoring examples improve probability estimates, which supports giving the agent a reference-range lookup instead of asking it to recall rates.
